chapter: Taxi dance job and the Fiesta
title: Hours, ticket rules and closing of the taxi dance hall
summary: Pay was good but the hours brutal; musicians played two choruses a dance, patrons bought tickets, and the hall was shut during the war over watered-down drinks.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Dance halls, lake resorts and where bands played

blocks.x: Worked for me at that time. Yeah. 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, you know. It was good pay. Oh, yeah. It was good pay, but Lord, hours.
Well, they gave you a lot of rest there, didn't they? Rest? What rest? Rest! Did you hear the man say a Jitney dance? Yeah. Rest. Lord, have fun.

Man, man. Boy, I was young, I could take it. From 8 to 4, 5 on Sunday mornings, 5 and 6. That's right. Mardi Gras Day from 9 to 3 and 4 the next Ash Wednesday. Oh, that was it. We'd get a break break from about 6 to 7, 30, Mardi Gras Day. It was a break to get something to eat. One guy had to go eat at the time, you know. You see the sandwich and trumpet players, man. Raymond Blount would play drum while I eat. He'd jump on the piano, play a little piano. He's a nice arranger. He'd play a little piano while Lewis gave us eat. Boy, that was rough.
Was it a tough place too? Or any fights? We had a police. Oh, yeah.

I didn't have a fight. But, man, it was a rough job. I'll tell you what. I couldn't take that no longer. No, I wouldn't do. One thing, you played anything you wanted. You played two foxtrots and a waltz, you see. So you played a fast one and a swing and a waltz. All night, that's what you had to play. Two choruses. And your dime was gone. And that's all. Some guys would get tickets, man, along with the longest desk. They liked the good, you know. They want to talk to us. They allowed them to talk, you know. No company. You couldn't sit down and hold no conversation. That didn't go. Just damage. You had to hold no conversation. If he sat down and talked, if he stand up and talked, you better buy some tickets. Every time that band play a tune, the band come around and get a ticket. She couldn't sit down and hold no conversation. He had to buy some tickets. That's right. Just like she was dancing. Every time they played a dance, they'd come to your table and get a ticket. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. You know, they wouldn't do it. Oh, Mr. Palama was the boss. Gus and Palama. One was a Greek, one was Italian. Now that was a combination. But they made money. Very nice. Sure was nice. Very nice. When we got off from there in the morning, they had a window fan, you know, right over the bandstand. And, man, we was, looked like we was rolling dust. Especially if it rained, you know, seeing people coming in and dancing and all that mud come off and turning to dust, you see. Looked like we'd been on the highways. Oh, that was some rough time, I'm telling you. I couldn't take that. Now, I wish you'd see the taxi dance when I first started working at my job, that job I had 10 years. It was a taxi. But I wish you'd seen that taxi. Man, we played one or two numbers and stopped five minutes. That's right. We didn't play like no taxi dance back like here. We didn't do it. And people coming in, we used to taxi dance from Los Angeles and things. They say, man, this is a taxi dance. You all get all that rest. I say, sure. And we didn't play for four hours, eight to twelve. Curfew, you know. One o'clock on Saturday. And then the war broke out. The guards was, looked like robbing the boys, I don't know, some kind of humbug dead with the army. So they made them cut out the taxi dance. Oh, they got them on that B drinking. That's what they got us on. Yeah, they closed us up for a while. On that B drinking, see. Of course, it was nothing but coke. That's why I'm charging for whiskey. And they caught on to it, she said. Nothing but coke, the old gal said. Give me a double one. She say, yeah. Honey, you mind buying me a drink? He said, yeah. Oh, she said, well, I want a double drink. That little whiskey they put in there. That ain't nothing. And she's slick, you see. She wouldn't ever let him smell it, you see. You know, the soon the waiter sat down, she'd drink it right down, you see. Yeah, she would never let him smell it. Some of them would want to smell it, you see. See, was it whiskey? Oh, he wouldn't do that. No, soon that waiter sat that glass down there. That was done. That's right. So some plainclothes guys coming out the army and caught on to it, you see. Two of them sat at the table and when she went to grab the glass, they took it with another thing, you see. And they smelled it, you see. I don't want that but coke and ice. Close my boss up, throw him off. Put him off limits. Might as well close when he put it on, cause that's a soldier town, you see. Mm-hmm. And knocked him out. He had to pull some strings to get back, cause he never would've got back. But by him knowing some big shots now pass, I would've put him back. Right. And they couldn't serve them a beach ranch, you see. Mm-hmm. Them girls made money. Yeah, they made money. They really did. Cause we were the only joint in town and they'd run dance every night, you see. Seven nights a week.
